expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation not to pay the bonus 100% on adjusted EBITDA and explains what that would reward, such as cutting people, training, maintenance or quality.
expectations.evidence: Opens: 'I'd draft the plan with EBITDA as the largest weight (50%) but not 100%, and with restructuring costs counted in the bonus number, not excluded.' Explains: 'A bonus on EBITDA alone also pays for cutting training, security and maintenance this year and leaves the bill to the next owner.'

expectations.text: The reply proposes a balanced scorecard with customer, people and quality or risk measures (patient safety or product quality in this sector) alongside honest financial measures, with weights.
expectations.evidence: Weighted table: Bonus EBITDA 50%, Cash conversion 15%, Net revenue retention / churn 15%, Regretted attrition and engagement 10%, 'Quality and safety (uptime, security incidents, open patient-safety or compliance findings)' 10%.

expectations.text: The reply challenges excluding restructuring costs as one-off after three years of restructuring, and defines the profit measure honestly.
expectations.evidence: 'Restructuring, severance, advisory and related costs are INCLUDED (deducted). Restructuring has occurred in each of the last three years, so it is a cost of running this business, not a one-off.' Only a 'genuinely single event' may be excluded, up to a 2% cap. 'Savings are credited only net of their full cost'.

expectations.text: The reply adds a multi-year element, malus or clawback, and guards against gaming the measures.
expectations.evidence: '30% deferred and vesting equally over the next 2 years'. 'Deferred amounts can be reduced (malus), and paid amounts recovered (clawback) for 3 years'. Each scorecard measure has a 'Gaming risk and guard' column (independent survey, incident review by the risk owner, normalised payables).

expectations.text: The reply puts leaders' accountability first: no bonus for headcount reduction as such, and leadership bonuses cut first when results disappoint.
expectations.evidence: 'No bonus is paid for headcount reduction as such. If EBITDA misses threshold, executive bonuses go first, before any involuntary reductions are considered.' Section 8: 'executive team pay and bonus are reduced first and by the largest percentage'.

expectations.text: The reply makes the case in the owners' terms (value at exit: retained customers, recurring revenue, capable teams) and delivers a usable draft plan.
expectations.evidence: 'the multiple depends on retained recurring revenue and a stable team, so the other 50% protects the thing they're selling'. 'A buyer pays for retained recurring revenue'. The draft is usable: scorecard, definition, gates, deferral, malus, leaders-first, governance, open items.

overall_quality.evidence: Concise, balanced and well guarded. But it overstates the SEC rule, leaves most thresholds 'set from budget', and labels a 'no payout above target' rule as an all-or-nothing gate.

factual_errors.evidence: 'If you were SEC-registered, the non-GAAP rules would bar this exclusion outright' is wrong. Reg S-K Item 10(e)(1)(ii)(B) bars labelling a recurring charge as non-recurring, and SEC C&DI 102.03 says the adjustment itself is still allowed. The rules also govern non-GAAP disclosures, not bonus plan definitions.

skill_leak.evidence: plan.md: 'the playbook-style norm is 3 years for the deferred share' refers to a playbook or reference source the user hasn't seen (mild).

owns_result.evidence: Leaders carry the downside first, but it never says the past restructurings are leadership's responsibility.

best_insight.value: Ask whether the last three restructurings actually paid back net of cost and rehires. That answer decides whether any allowance for restructuring is justified.

suggestions.assertion: The reply adds a multi-year element, malus or clawback, and guards against gaming the measures.
suggestions.reason: The wording 'a multi-year element, malus or clawback' can be read as three requirements or as 'a multi-year element such as malus or clawback'. Samples with clawback but no deferral (C, E, H) pass or fail depending on the reading. Name the requirements separately.

suggestions.assertion: The reply puts leaders' accountability first: no bonus for headcount reduction as such, and leadership bonuses cut first when results disappoint.
suggestions.reason: 'Leadership bonuses cut first' needs a bar. A cap at target in redundancy years (F) or a 'mandatory downward review' (H) is much weaker than releasing the management accrual before any role is cut (B) or zeroing executive pools first (D, I, J). Say what counts.

suggestions.assertion: The reply challenges excluding restructuring costs as one-off after three years of restructuring, and defines the profit measure honestly.
suggestions.reason: 'Defines the profit measure honestly' is met by capped or allowance-based add-backs (C, G) that still let savings count while part of the cost is excluded. Consider requiring that no cost is excluded while its savings are counted (symmetry).

No assertion checks that worked examples add up, or that hard gates don't create perverse effects. Zero bonus on any involuntary reduction (A, I) can deter a needed change or encourage disguised exits. A seasoned CFO would weigh both.

eval_feedback.overall: 6/6 on assertions. One factual overstatement about SEC rules.
